title: The birth of electronic music
subject: art
description: From Theremin to the clubs of Chicago and Detroit, electronic music invents sounds without an orchestra and transforms world dance.

hero.hook: From laboratories to dancefloors: how machines invented new music.

blocks.text: Electronic music doesn't start in nightclubs. It is born in laboratories, when inventors look for sounds that are impossible to get from a violin or a piano.

From the  of the 1920s to the  and the , one idea spans the century: the machine can create, not just record. Today, it structures a large part of world pop and . [[The Theremin]] [[Chicago house]] [[Chicago house and Detroit techno]] [[charts]]

sections.title: The pioneers: from Theremin to musique concrete

blocks.text: In **1920**, the Russian inventor **Leon Theremin** (Lev Termen) designed the : a device played without contact. Hands move near antennas in an electromagnetic field. The sound glides, almost vocal, and soon haunts science fiction films. [[The Theremin]]

blocks.caption: The Theremin: an instrument played in the air, without touching the strings.

blocks.text: After 1945, research changed terrain. In Paris, on public radio, **Pierre Schaeffer** and **Peter Henry** invented musique concrete: recording everyday noises, then cutting them, inverting them, looping them on magnetic tape. In Cologne, other studios prefer pure synthesis: sounds born from oscillators, without an acoustic source. These two paths still underpin current production: on one side , on the other synthesis. [[sampling]]
Theremin presented his instrument to Lenin. Fascinated, the Soviet leader reportedly requested hundreds of copies to spread technical modernity in the USSR.

sections.title: The Moog, Wendy Carlos and Kraftwerk

blocks.text: In the 1960s, the American engineer **Robert Moog** miniaturized the synthesizer with transistors. In **1968**, **Wendy Carlos**'s album *Switched-On Bach* proves that electronics can carry classical complexity. The gadget becomes an instrument.

blocks.caption: The Moog synthesizer: the machine leaves the lab for the studio.

blocks.text: In Düsseldorf, the German group **Kraftwerk**, founded by **Ralf Hütter** and **Florian Schneider**, imposes cold and repetitive pop. With *Autobahn* (**1974**) and *The Man-Machine* (**1978**), they sing about the highway, the robot, the city. Their rhythm would later nourish American hip-hop and European dance music.

blocks.caption: Kraftwerk: the man-machine as artistic persona.

blocks.text: On certain tours, Kraftwerk sent mannequins in their likeness for press conferences, pushing the concept of man-machine to the limit.

In the 1980s, affordable machines like the **Roland TR-808** drum machine changed the game. In Chicago, in clubs frequented by black and gay communities, DJ **Frankie Knuckles** refines the : regular 4/4 rhythm, warmth inherited from disco. [[Chicago house]]

In **Detroit**, a city marked by the decline of automobile factories, three university friends (**Juan Atkins**, **Derrick May**, **Kevin Saunderson**) invent a darker aesthetic: the . Exported to Europe, it found a strong echo in Berlin after the fall of the Wall. [[Chicago house and Detroit techno]]
The TR-808 was a commercial failure: the pros found it “unrealistic”. Sold second-hand, it becomes the weapon of Chicago's broke DJs.

From the 1990s,  (computer-assisted music) transformed a simple PC into a studio. Electronics leaves the club for advertising, cinema and almost all pop.  remain the roots of a global language. [[computer music software]] [[Chicago house and Detroit techno]]
